source: https://elibrary.maff.gov.kh/assets/files/books/a4cc69c087a47633f2aec73f8c462b801626315648.pdf (Khmer translation of an IRRI rice growth/physiology primer, credited to Dr. B.S. Vergara)
text: Before harvest, a farmer can estimate the coming grain yield in a field using a simple counting method rather than waiting to find out at threshing. First, count the number of productive hills (clumps of rice) per square meter: mark out a 1x1 meter square in a representative part of the field (not an unusually good or bad patch) and count the hills inside it; this count depends directly on planting spacing -- for example, a spacing of 25x25 cm gives about 16 hills per square meter, while a tighter 20x20 cm spacing gives about 25 hills per square meter, following the simple relationship that hills per square meter equals 1 divided by (spacing in meters squared). Second, count the average number of productive tillers (panicle-bearing stems) per hill by sampling several hills and averaging -- a well-managed crop commonly has around 16-17 productive tillers per hill in the source's worked example, giving roughly 270 or more panicles per square meter when multiplied by the hill count. Third, estimate the average number of filled grains per panicle by threshing out a sample of panicles by hand and counting -- a healthy panicle commonly holds somewhere in the range of 250-300 grains. Multiplying hills per square meter, by tillers (panicles) per hill, by grains per panicle gives an estimate of total grains per square meter, which can then be converted to a yield figure per hectare using the known weight of a standard number of grains (thousand-grain weight) for the variety being grown. This method will not be exact, since it depends on how representative the sampled hills and panicles are, but it gives a farmer a much better pre-harvest estimate than guessing, and can also help flag early whether a field is falling short of its expected yield potential in time to investigate the cause.
